questions.question: How does Show-o generate an image with masked discrete diffusion?
options: Decode continuous pixels with a separate diffusion model and no shared transformer.
Sample one codebook token and copy it across every image position.
Generate every image token autoregressively from left to right.
Start with masked image tokens, predict them in parallel, and iteratively keep confident tokens.
questions.explanation: Show-o starts with every image token masked, predicts masked positions in parallel, commits the most confident tokens, and repeats until the sequence is filled. Left-to-right decoding would require a sequential pass per token and is the alternative it improves on.

questions.question: What attention mask does Show-o use for a mixed text and image-token sequence?
options: Bidirectional attention over all text and image tokens in the sequence.
Causal attention over image tokens and no attention over text tokens.
Separate masks that prevent any text-image interaction.
Causal attention over text and bidirectional attention within an image block.
questions.explanation: Text tokens retain causal attention so next-token prediction cannot see future text; image tokens within the same block attend bidirectionally to support simultaneous masked-token recovery. Making all text bidirectional would leak future text targets.

questions.question: Which statement distinguishes Show-o's image sampling from Chameleon or Emu3?
options: Show-o fills masked image tokens in parallel over a small number of iterations.
Show-o predicts each image token sequentially with one pass per token.
Show-o uses continuous image patches and a separate text model.
Show-o requires a new model checkpoint for inpainting.
questions.explanation: Show-o uses MaskGIT-style masked prediction, filling many image positions per transformer pass over roughly 8–16 iterations. Chameleon or Emu3 generates image tokens autoregressively, requiring a sequential step for each token.

questions.question: Why does Show-o support image inpainting without a separate training objective?
options: The model copies unmasked pixels into the missing region.
The model uses an image classifier to label each masked patch.
The text decoder predicts image pixels from a diffusion schedule.
The same masked-token prediction objective learns to fill missing image tokens.
questions.explanation: Training on random masked subsets teaches the model to recover missing image tokens from visible context. Inpainting supplies a partially masked image and uses the same prediction task; copying visible pixels cannot infer the hidden region.

questions.question: A product needs one open checkpoint for VQA, text-to-image, and inpainting with relatively fast generation. Which model family fits the lesson's recommendation?
options: Show-o, which combines understanding and masked discrete image generation.
A pure Chameleon decoder, which generates images autoregressively only.
Transfusion, which uses continuous images and a two-loss diffusion objective.
CLIP, which returns image-text similarity without image generation.
questions.explanation: Show-o combines VQA and text generation with text-to-image and inpainting using one checkpoint and masked discrete image sampling. Transfusion is also unified but uses continuous-image diffusion/flow and a more complex two-loss training path.

questions.question: Image quality is the highest priority and extra training complexity is acceptable. Which alternative does the lesson favor over Show-o?
options: A CLIP dual encoder, because retrieval embeddings directly render pixels.
Show-o with one sampling step, because parallel prediction is exact.
Transfusion or MMDiT, which use continuous image representations and diffusion/flow.
Chameleon, because VQ quantization has no reconstruction ceiling.
questions.explanation: For maximum image fidelity with added training complexity acceptable, Transfusion/MMDiT keep image representations continuous and train diffusion or flow objectives. Show-o is faster, but its discrete tokenizer imposes a reconstruction ceiling.
